content: 1. Some interpretations suggest that Hell represents the unavoidable presence of God experienced in the absence of love for Him. Others propose that Hell signifies the complete annihilation of both the physical body and spiritual existence. 2. In Roman Catholic theology, Purgatory is described as a supernatural realm where souls who have died in a state of grace but still need to atone for venial sins or temporal punishments due to past sins are purified before entering Heaven. 3. Jehovah's Witnesses interpret the term soul (nephesh or psyche) in the Bible as referring to a person, an animal, or the life they possess. They believe the soul is not a separate part of a human but the entirety of a living being. Consequently, when a person or animal dies, the soul ceases to exist, as supported by Ezekiel 18:4. They view Hell (Hades or Sheol) not as a place of fiery torment but as the common grave of humankind, a state of unconsciousness. After the final judgment, the righteous are expected to receive eternal life and live forever in a paradise on Earth. A select group, referred to as the little flock of 144,000 individuals, will attain immortality and ascend to Heaven to rule as kings and priests. Jehovah's Witnesses distinguish between eternal life, which can end (though not due to disease or aging), and immortality, which is absolute and cannot be terminated by any means. They teach that Jesus was the first to be granted heavenly immortality, and Revelation 7:4 and 14:1, 3 refer to a literal number of 144,000 additional individuals who will become self-sustaining, requiring nothing external to sustain their lives. 4. In Mormon theology, the afterlife is divided into three degrees of glory: the Celestial Kingdom, the Terrestrial Kingdom, and the Telestial Kingdom. These are the eternal dwelling places for nearly all who have lived on Earth. Those who do not inherit any degree of glory, despite being resurrected, reside in a state called outer darkness. This state is not considered a degree of glory and is reserved for individuals known as Sons of Perdition. Critics of the Latter-Day Saint movement argue that Joseph Smith, its founder, drew upon the ideas of Emanuel Swedenborg to develop the concept of the three degrees of glory. 5. The doctrine of conditional immortality posits that the human soul is naturally mortal and that immortality is a gift granted by God. This view, though a minority within evangelical circles, has gained traction in recent years. Some groups that adhere to the doctrine of baptismal regeneration also believe in a third realm called Limbo, which is the final destination for souls who were not baptized but were innocent of mortal sin. This includes unbaptized infants and virtuous individuals who were never exposed to Christianity during their lifetimes. Christian Scientists hold that sin brought death into existence and that death will be overcome when sin is eradicated. 6. In Islam, it is believed that every individual possesses an immortal soul that continues to exist after death. Souls that have led evil lives undergo correction in Hell, after which they may be admitted to Heaven. However, souls guilty of unforgivable evil remain in Hell eternally and never experience Heaven. 7. The concept of clinical immortality raises numerous ethical, medical, philosophical, and religious questions. These include issues related to persistent vegetative states, the continuity of personality over time, the development of technologies to replicate or mimic the mind, social and economic disparities caused by extended lifespans, and the survival of humanity in the face of the eventual heat death of the universe. 8. Many of the world's religions include doctrines of an eternal afterlife. Narratives from Christianity and Islam suggest that eternal afterlife is undesirable for the unfaithful. For example, in Christianity, the story of the rich man and Lazarus illustrates the torment of the unfaithful in Hell, contrasted with the comfort of the faithful in Heaven. Similarly, Islamic teachings describe the eternal suffering of the wretched in Hell and the eternal bliss of the blessed in Paradise. In Buddhism, the concept of eternal rebirth is seen as an undesirable condition caused by ignorance, which must be overcome. Physical immortality has also been imagined as a form of eternal torment, as depicted in Mary Shelley's short story The Mortal Immortal, where the protagonist witnesses the death of everyone he loves. Jorge Luis Borges explored the idea that life derives its meaning from death in his short story The Immortal, where a society that achieves immortality finds time infinite and motivation for action absent. 9. Many religions promise their adherents an eternal paradise in the afterlife, characterized by perfection as part of a divine plan, making it categorically desirable. Physical immortality is often considered preferable to death, which has been inevitable for all humans thus far. However, this presumes tolerable living conditions, as evidenced by the prevalence of suicide in intolerable circumstances. 10. Numerous symbols represent immortality. For example, the Egyptian ankh, often depicted in the hands of gods and pharaohs, symbolizes life and immortality, signifying control over the journey of life. Another symbol of immortality is the Möbius strip in the shape of a trefoil knot.
